title: Author a module
description: Add a small reusable task to your blueprint, declare what it changes, and check it on the right host before provisioning.

sections.title: Pick the smallest payload
sections.text: Pick the smallest payload Choose a module when you need to install packages or run a task independently of your other setup. Start with a package list when that expresses the whole job. Use a script for behavior that needs logic, and attach a manifest to document trust and declare implementations for additional adapters. Payload Use it for brewfile Homebrew bundles on hosts with Homebrew. packages Package lists for Debian-based hosts. <module-name>.sh Shell-driven setup. module.toml Trust metadata and adapter implementations.

sections.title: Choose a host bucket and name
sections.text:
Choose a host bucket and name Put shared modules in dotfiles/modules/universal and host-specific modules in macos, debian, or arch under dotfiles/modules. Give the script the same basename as its directory. This example uses the universal module name local-check and prints a single line as its smoke test. The module name accepted by smu is relative to its host bucket. If you use a nested location such as universal/editor/local-check, use editor/local-check when calling smu. #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

printf '%s\n' 'local-check module ran'

sections.title: Describe side effects in the manifest
sections.text:
Describe side effects in the manifest Save this manifest beside the script. Match network, sudo, and write declarations to what the module actually does. The example script prints a message and has no uninstall script, so its rollback classification is manual. When a script module does install files, keep repeated runs predictable. Check whether a change is already in place before writing it, quote paths, and handle failures explicitly. Add a <module-name>.uninstall.sh only when you can reverse the specific changes the module owns. id = "local-check"
trust = "first-party"
network = false
requires_sudo = false
writes = []
rollback = "manual"

sections.title: Use script hooks for separate steps
sections.text: Use script hooks for separate steps A script module can have before.sh and after.sh in the same directory. Keep hooks small and review them along with the module. The installer runs each hook and the module script in its own Bash process, so shared inputs should come from explicit files or environment variables available to all three processes.

sections.title: Check discovery and review the plan
sections.text:
Check discovery and review the plan Run from the installed blueprint. Check the script’s syntax, confirm the module is visible, and read its trust report and plan. A shell script can perform behavior the plan cannot infer from its contents, so read the script and hooks even if the plan looks routine. bash -n dotfiles/modules/universal/local-check/local-check.sh
smu --list-modules --search local-check
smu trust doctor local-check --json
smu diff local-check

sections.title: Run the module on a test machine
sections.text: Run the module on a test machine Use a disposable test environment or an appropriate test machine for a module that changes the host. This command selects the new module and skips the base setup. For the example, expect the line local-check module ran. After the test, run it again and compare the result. If you add the module to a blueprint profile, rerun that profile’s adapter preflight to check the combined set. smu --provision --no-base --modules local-check Select and apply modules Compose a blueprint profile

title: Blueprints
description: A blueprint is the Git repository that describes your setup. Fork the template and keep machine configuration under version control.

sections.title: Blueprint layout
sections.text: Blueprint layout The set-me-up blueprint template ships example dotfiles, a custom module, and the entry point that delegates to the installer. Fork the template so the branch you install points to configuration you control. A blueprint is the configuration and checkout manifest. The installer submodule provides the CLI, and shared module repositories supply work the blueprint can reuse. Path Purpose smu.toml Choose the provisioning adapter and profile modules. dotfiles/tag-example/ Start from an example rcm tag. dotfiles/rcrc Choose rcm dotfile directories and behavior. dotfiles/modules/example/ Start from an example custom module. dotfiles/modules/install.sh Bootstrap the chosen blueprint. .gitmodules Declare the installer and shared module checkouts.

sections.title: Pick a provisioning adapter
sections.text:
Pick a provisioning adapter A profile lists modules for a setup. This example selects the traditional rcm adapter and the module shipped in the blueprint template. The global provisioning setting picks the default adapter. A named profile can select its own modules and override that adapter. Use the exact module names in the checkout and validate the profile on a host it is meant to support. [provisioning]
adapter = "rcm"

[profile.default]
modules = ["example"] Provisioning adapters

sections.title: Validate the blueprint
sections.text:
Validate the blueprint Use the bundled CLI from Quick start. The blueprint doctor checks the repository and configuration, and adapter preflight checks whether the selected modules can be handled by the adapter on this host. The example assumes the stock rcm profile. For a different blueprint, substitute its configured adapter and profile. If preflight reports a missing module, check the name and whether its submodule was initialized. A missing adapter means the selected module needs an implementation for that adapter. smu blueprint doctor --strict --json
smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter rcm --profile default --json

sections.title: Track what changes
sections.text: Track what changes Keep your customizations in your fork and review upstream changes before updating. Keep machine secrets out of version control. The installer fast-forwards a clean existing checkout and refuses to update a dirty one by default. Review a pull request as you would a code change. Check the scripts, package list, expected writes, and any submodule revision changes. For an rcm setup, keep the checkout at its original path after symlinking dotfiles. Install the fork Update a setup Customize dotfiles Author a module

sections.title: Understand what each repository owns
sections.text: Understand what each repository owns Your blueprint records the configuration you intend to use. The bundled installer interprets that configuration and provides smu. Shared module repositories contain implementations that can evolve independently. Keeping these responsibilities separate makes it possible to review a module update without confusing it with a change to your own dotfiles. A submodule reference records a commit, not a promise to follow the latest upstream branch. Review both the reference change in the blueprint and the code at the new commit. Commit your own changes in the repository that owns those files; committing only the parent repository does not save uncommitted edits inside a submodule. From versioned intent to applied setup Blueprint Installer Modules   Provide configuration and pinned sources   Resolve selected implementations   Report execution results   Record the applied setup event The blueprint owns your choices; the installer and module checkouts supply their implementations.

sections.title: Review a blueprint change before installing it
sections.text: Review a blueprint change before installing it Read a change in terms of what it will do on a machine. A small profile edit can select a large package collection, and a short submodule reference update can contain many script changes. Compare the target machine, adapter, module selection, and destination paths before treating a diff as routine. Keep changes focused enough to test on one host. Add one module or dotfile tag, preview its effects, and verify the application that consumes it. This produces a useful checkpoint before you expand the setup to another machine. Inspect changed scripts and hooks, not only configuration values. Check package sources, privilege requirements, and writes outside the checkout. Keep secrets and machine-specific credentials out of commits. Run blueprint doctor and the applicable adapter preflight on the target host. Review a plan

title: Organize and link dotfiles
description: Use rcm tags to choose which configuration files a blueprint links into your home directory.

sections.title: When to use an rcm tag
sections.text: When to use an rcm tag Use a tag when several machines share a blueprint but need different configuration files. The tag stores files in Git and rcm creates links in the user’s home directory. Editing a linked file may also edit the tracked file in your blueprint, so check the link before making a machine-local change. These steps use the rcm provisioning path. For a Nix-backed setup, decide which files Home Manager owns before adding matching rcm paths. A path has one owner during normal provisioning. Choose an adapter Blueprint layout

sections.title: Choose a tag and map the paths
sections.text:
Choose a tag and map the paths In your blueprint, create a directory such as dotfiles/tag-work and put configuration files inside it using the same layout as the rest of the dotfiles tree. The example below gives Git a configuration file and a separate, tool-specific file under the home directory’s .config tree. The rcm configuration in your blueprint is dotfiles/rcrc. Add work to TAGS before the existing example and smu tags if work should take precedence. Keep the EXCLUDES value already used by your blueprint. Source path Home path dotfiles/tag-work/gitconfig ~/.gitconfig dotfiles/tag-work/config/example-tool/settings ~/.config/example-tool/settings TAGS="work example smu"
EXCLUDES="base modules utilities"

sections.title: Keep overlapping files intentional
sections.text: Keep overlapping files intentional A tagged file replaces the file at the same destination as a whole. If you copy Git settings into a tag, include the shared settings you still need. A work-specific tag is a useful place for configuration you want to share across work machines. Keep credentials and machine-local values outside the repository. For tools that support include files, store only a reference to a local file in the blueprint and create the local file separately.

sections.title: Keep per-host files out of commits
sections.text:
Keep per-host files out of commits For an installed blueprint with machine-local support, run smu local init to prepare local configuration paths. Place host-specific files under dotfiles/local and add the local tag to dotfiles/rcrc. Keep the directory ignored by Git so a local setting does not enter the shared blueprint by mistake. Initialization creates a local folder and starter files when they are missing. Follow it with smu local doctor to check the local paths, rcm tag, and changes that still block an update. After adding a local file, preview the links the same way you would for shared files. smu local init
smu local doctor --json

sections.title: Review the link plan
sections.text: Review the link plan Run the preview after changing tags or adding files. It uses the installed blueprint’s dotfiles/rcrc. Compare each affected source and destination with what you intended, especially files already present in your home directory. If a destination already contains a regular file or a link you manage yourself, compare and back up its content before applying. The set-me-up wrapper invokes rcup with force. smu --lsrc

sections.title: Apply and verify the links
sections.text:
Apply and verify the links Apply only after reviewing the preview. Then check the destination link and open the tool that uses it. For the Git example, the target should point into the active blueprint. smu --rcup
ls -l "$HOME/.gitconfig"

sections.title: Diagnose a missing or unexpected link
sections.text: Diagnose a missing or unexpected link If the destination is missing, check the tag spelling, its position in TAGS, the path inside the tag, and any EXCLUDES entries. If the source is from another checkout, check SMU_HOME_DIR and run the preview again. The smu --rcdn command removes managed dotfile links. Treat it as a broad change to the current set of links and review the scope before running it. If you only changed a tag, fix the tag and verify the resulting link plan first. Troubleshoot an installed setup Review paths and secrets

sections.title: Understand the lifetime of a managed link
sections.text: Understand the lifetime of a managed link In the rcm flow, your home-directory entry points back to a file inside the blueprint checkout. Editing the source changes what the application reads through that link. Deleting or moving the checkout can therefore break configuration even though the destination link still appears in your home directory. Keep the active checkout at a stable path. When adopting existing dotfiles, compare their content before moving them into a tag. Test one representative file first so that tag selection, exclusions, and the link destination are all understood. From a tag to a live configuration file Blueprint tag rcm preview Home directory   Select tagged source files   Inspect intended destinations   Apply reviewed symlinks The destination remains dependent on the source file in the active checkout.

sections.title: Verify the application, not just the symlink
sections.text: Verify the application, not just the symlink A correct link is only the first check. Configuration can contain absolute paths, commands that are not installed yet, or plugins that load on startup. Open a new shell or restart the consuming application and check its behavior before deleting your backup. For a failed application start, separate link selection from application syntax. Confirm where the link points, read the source file, and then use the application’s own configuration check when it provides one. This avoids changing rcm settings to solve an unrelated syntax error. Move to another machine

title: Plan a fleet of hosts
description: Review a consistent set of per-host smu plans before making changes across multiple machines.

sections.title: Pick the hosts and profile first
sections.text: Pick the hosts and profile first Use fleet planning when you maintain multiple hosts and want to review which plan each host would run. Group similar machines together so each command uses the intended profile and provisioning adapter. Keep a staging or test host separate from the rest. Check the built-in profile and the adapter requirements on each host family. For the VPS example, use Debian or Ubuntu hosts that already have smu available to their SSH user. Choose a machine profile Prepare a headless VPS

sections.title: Write the host list explicitly
sections.text:
Write the host list explicitly Use one host per line followed by its SSH user. Blank lines and lines beginning with # are ignored. The examples below are placeholders. Replace them with the names and users you intend to check. Always supply the user. A line without a user defaults to root. If the file is missing, smu generates a localhost entry, so check the host count and names before relying on the plan. staging.example.test deploy
worker-01.example.test deploy

sections.title: Review the generated commands
sections.text: Review the generated commands Fleet plan builds a report locally. Each command entry identifies a host, user, proposed smu plan command, and path for a possible log. Compare the commands with your intended SSH targets and confirm the provisioning adapter is valid for those hosts. This example specifies rcm explicitly so the plan does not inherit the controller’s configured adapter. Substitute the adapter you intend to check. smu fleet plan --hosts hosts.txt --profile vps --provisioning-adapter rcm --json

sections.title: Check the remote execution inputs
sections.text: Check the remote execution inputs The dry run reports the apply request without opening SSH sessions. In the JSON, verify the commands, run ID, and executes_remote value. The generated command is smu plan, a read-only description of what the host’s setup would do. For an actual remote plan collection, the SSH user needs key-based access, a trusted host key, and smu on the noninteractive PATH. Check a single host first and review its output before extending the host list. smu fleet apply --hosts hosts.txt --profile vps --provisioning-adapter rcm --dry-run --json

sections.title: Review results before provisioning
sections.text: Review results before provisioning Use the plan output to check the expected modules, secrets findings, dotfile conflicts, and rollback coverage for each machine. Resolve failures on the affected host. A missing smu in a noninteractive session calls for a PATH check, and an SSH failure calls for reviewing the hostname, user, and credentials. Apply the appropriate setup or adapter command on each host only after reviewing its plan. Start on the staging host, verify the packages or application that changed, and carry the same checks to the next host. Diagnose a host Check plan and trust findings

title: Choose machine profiles
description: Separate built-in machine presets from blueprint profiles so you can preview the right modules and adapter for each host.

sections.title: Two kinds of profile
sections.text: Two kinds of profile A built-in machine profile is a preset defined by smu. It describes a machine role, default modules and adapter, submodule scope, and safety defaults. A blueprint profile is a named table in your own smu.toml. It lets you version module selections and adapter overrides alongside your dotfiles. Task Command Inspect a built-in role smu machine-profile show vps --json Plan using a built-in role smu plan --machine vps --json Preflight a named blueprint profile smu provisioning-adapter preflight --profile lab --json

sections.title: Inspect the available presets
sections.text:
Inspect the available presets Use the list command to get the IDs shipped with your installed version. The show command includes the proposed module list and safety settings. Pick the role closest to the host and confirm its modules are available in your blueprint. The built-in vps, ci, and agent-host setup paths require Debian-based systems. smu machine-profile list --json
smu machine-profile show vps --json

sections.title: Preview a built-in role on the host
sections.text: Preview a built-in role on the host Run the plan on the machine you intend to configure. A machine preset supplies an adapter default to the plan, and the --provisioning-adapter option lets you compare another choice. For example, inspect the same Debian VPS modules with the rcm adapter used by a traditional blueprint. In the result, review provisioning.modules and provisioning.adapter, then look at dotfile conflicts, secret findings, trust warnings, and rollback coverage. Treat the plan as a review artifact before running the actual setup. smu plan --machine vps --provisioning-adapter rcm --json Set up a Debian or Ubuntu VPS

sections.title: Keep a custom profile in the blueprint
sections.text:
Keep a custom profile in the blueprint Add a profile for a repeatable combination of modules. This example keeps the stock blueprint’s example module in the default profile and creates a lab profile with the same module. Once it works, add modules that your own lab needs. Choose the module names from smu --list-modules on the target host. A profile can override the global adapter, so keep its module set compatible with that adapter. [provisioning]
adapter = "rcm"

[profile.default]
modules = ["example"]

[profile.lab]
adapter = "rcm"
modules = ["example"]

sections.title: Validate the custom profile
sections.text: Validate the custom profile Preflight with the same profile name you will use when applying the adapter. Check the module coverage and the proposed command. An unknown built-in role from smu machine-profile show indicates that you passed an ID outside the built-in list. Use the adapter preflight’s --profile argument for names declared in smu.toml. smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter rcm --profile lab --json Provisioning adapters Manage a blueprint fork

sections.title: Design profiles around machine responsibilities
sections.text: Design profiles around machine responsibilities A profile should explain why a group of modules belongs together. A workstation may need interactive tools and application preferences; a headless server should avoid desktop assumptions. Reusing a module across both roles is appropriate only when its implementation supports both environments. Prefer a small shared baseline and explicit role-specific additions. Keep the profile in the blueprint so reviewers can see how a module-selection change affects each machine. Names such as lab are examples from your configuration, not built-in smu machine IDs. Choose the role, then validate its implementation Machine role Blueprint profile Adapter preflight   Select the intended module set   Check adapter coverage on this host   Review readiness before applying Built-in presets and named blueprint profiles are distinct inputs; validate the choice you actually intend to apply.

sections.title: Review a profile again on a different host
sections.text: Review a profile again on a different host A configuration that works on one computer is evidence about that computer. Operating-system packages, architecture, permissions, and existing files can differ on the next host. Run discovery and preflight there instead of assuming that a shared profile makes the environment identical. If a module is unavailable, confirm its checkout and supported host bucket before substituting another one. Record intentional platform differences in configuration rather than making unexplained local edits. Prepare a new machine

title: Modules
description: Discover modules in your blueprint, inspect what they do, and apply the subset you need.

sections.title: Discover modules
sections.text:
Discover modules smu looks under dotfiles/modules in the installed blueprint. It lists modules by operating system bucket and includes universal modules in the usual host view. Output lists the relative name and a marker such as script, brewfile, packages, or manifest. For a row under macos named productivity/hyperkey, pass productivity/hyperkey to smu. The --all switch widens discovery across buckets and does not make those modules compatible with this host. Use --search to filter names and smu status --search to check their install state. A module can be installed, missing, partial, or unknown. Unknown is common when a script provides no detection marker. smu --list-modules
smu --list-modules --search shell
smu status --search shell --json

sections.title: Preview module changes
sections.text: Preview module changes Check the module’s implementation before running it. The stock blueprint has a direct custom module at dotfiles/modules/example/example.sh. smu can resolve that module by name even if it is absent from the operating-system buckets in the discovery list. The diff reports whether a module would be installed or verified based on detected state. It also reports planned changes to generated adapter files. Use it with a source review because it does not execute the module or predict every package manager or script side effect. smu diff example

sections.title: Apply selected modules
sections.text: Apply selected modules Provision a reviewed module by name. The --no-base option excludes the base module from the requested list. If you intend to run the base setup, review it and select base explicitly. The example script is a template stub. It imports utilities from the default checkout path and has no package operations. The sample assumes that default path. Substitute a reviewed module from your own checkout when you are ready to apply real setup changes. smu --provision --no-base --modules example

sections.title: Verify the result
sections.text: Verify the result Read the provisioning summary and look for example in the successfully provisioned list. The stock example has no package or config output. Use the latest ledger event in smu status --json as an additional check. The module can be absent from the modules list because its directory is outside the OS buckets. For a package or script module listed under an OS bucket, check its status and inspect the affected package or file directly. A script without an installation marker can still show unknown after a successful run. If a module is missing, check its name relative to its OS bucket, the selected submodule scope, and the files present in the checkout. smu status --json Write detection and cleanup scripts Troubleshoot module discovery

sections.title: Preview an uninstall
sections.text: Preview an uninstall Brewfile and package modules can be reversed declaratively. Script modules need an opt-in uninstall script. Review the plan for items that need manual cleanup. The stock example has no uninstall companion, so the preview can report manual cleanup. For another module, substitute its name and inspect the list of actions before deciding whether to run the uninstall. smu --uninstall --modules example --dry-run Trust and safety

sections.title: Follow the module lifecycle
sections.text: Follow the module lifecycle Discovery, planning, execution, and verification answer different questions. Discovery tells you what is present in this checkout. A diff describes the supported plan and detected state. Provisioning runs the selected implementation. Verification confirms that the tool or file you needed actually works. Do not use an unknown status as a reason to repeatedly run a script. Some scripts have no installation marker, and a successful command can still leave an application that requires a restart or a separate sign-in. Read the module and verify its observable result. Select, inspect, apply, verify You smu Module   Discover and inspect a module   Return state and planned changes   Apply the reviewed selection   Execute the module implementation   Verify the resulting tool or file Planning helps review the operation; verification checks the result on the actual host.

sections.title: Expand your setup in small batches
sections.text: Expand your setup in small batches Start with one module whose effect you can check directly. If it installs a program, confirm the program starts and reports the expected version. If it writes configuration, inspect the path and launch the consuming application. Keep the previous working configuration until the new one is verified. Once the baseline works, add related modules in a separate change. This keeps failure reports useful: you can identify which batch changed the machine, rather than diagnosing an entire workstation at once. Build a repeatable routine

title: Move to a new machine
description: Use your existing blueprint to prepare another computer without copying stale state, credentials, or unsupported assumptions.

sections.title: Inventory the working setup
sections.text: Inventory the working setup Start from the machine that works. Save your blueprint changes in the appropriate repositories, including intentional submodule changes, and record the revision you want to reproduce. Keep a list of the applications and configuration that matter most to your daily work. Do not use the old machine’s home directory as a blind installation recipe. It can contain cached state, machine-specific paths, credentials, and files that were never managed by the blueprint. Identify which settings are versioned and which need a separate migration. Record the blueprint remote and revision. Review profile and module choices. List credentials that must be provisioned separately. Back up important personal files independently of setup configuration.

sections.title: Check the destination platform
sections.text: Check the destination platform Confirm the new machine’s operating system, architecture, package tools, and permissions. A blueprint shared between macOS and Linux can have different module implementations and package names. Discovery across all host buckets does not make a module compatible. Choose the installation destination before linking dotfiles, then keep that checkout path stable. For a headless Debian or Ubuntu host, follow the VPS guide rather than importing desktop assumptions. Choose profiles Prepare a VPS

sections.title: Install from reviewed sources
sections.text:
Install from reviewed sources Use the same download, inspection, and bootstrap preview procedure as a first installation. Confirm the fork, branch, destination, and submodule scope on this machine. A familiar repository name is not a substitute for reviewing the version being downloaded. Once installed, use the CLI pinned by the blueprint and check its help output. Run blueprint doctor before applying your normal selection. Preserve the preview output so you can compare what was intended with what was applied. smu blueprint doctor --strict --json
smu --list-modules Move intent, then verify on the new host Versioned blueprint New machine Verification   Install the reviewed checkout   Discover and preflight compatible modules   Apply a small baseline   Record intentional platform differences Reproduce versioned configuration; migrate private data and credentials through their own processes.

sections.title: Adopt configuration without losing local files
sections.text: Adopt configuration without losing local files Inspect files already present on the new machine before applying links. An application may have created useful defaults or a credential-bearing file. Compare the destination with the blueprint source and back it up before allowing replacement. Preview the rcm link plan, apply only after review, and inspect a representative link. Then start the consuming application in a new session. This catches missing executables and host-specific paths that a link check alone cannot detect. smu --lsrc

sections.title: Decide when the new machine is ready
sections.text: Decide when the new machine is ready Verify a short list of real tasks: open a fresh shell, run your editor, access the intended repositories, and use the applications that depend on your configuration. Test with the account and permissions you will actually use. Keep the old machine or its backup available until this checklist passes. Commit intentional fixes back to the blueprint so that the next installation benefits from what you learned. Leave credentials, caches, and temporary work out of those commits. Verify and maintain the setup

title: Migrate a blueprint toward Nix
description: Test a hybrid blueprint alongside an existing rcm setup and use coverage reports to decide which modules can move to Nix.

sections.title: Start with a working rcm blueprint
sections.text: Start with a working rcm blueprint A hybrid setup is useful when some modules already have a Nix implementation and others still rely on shell scripts or package lists. Begin from a working blueprint, record the modules you expect to keep, and make the migration on a Git branch or a separate test checkout. Install the Nix tooling required by your chosen adapter before testing the apply step. Home Manager manages user-level configuration, nix-darwin manages macOS system configuration, and the nixos adapter expects a NixOS host. Compare adapter support

sections.title: Compare coverage before editing
sections.text: Compare coverage before editing Run the migration comparison for the blueprint profile you want to move. It classifies modules as ported, partial, blocked, or kept-rcm. Use the module-level results to choose a small first batch and note any modules that need a new implementation. Keep a copy of the current report so you can compare it after changing manifests or module selections. smu nix migrate compare --profile default --json

sections.title: Generate a separate starter configuration
sections.text:
Generate a separate starter configuration Write the migration output to a fresh file in your test checkout. This creates a starter configuration so you can review it without overwriting your current smu.toml. Compare the files and carry over the existing profile module lists and any settings you still need. The hybrid example uses Home Manager for supported modules and allows rcm fallback for the remaining modules. Merge that adapter selection into the reviewed blueprint configuration before preflighting it. smu blueprint migrate --from rcm --to hybrid --output smu.hybrid.toml --json
git diff --no-index smu.toml smu.hybrid.toml

sections.title: Preflight the merged configuration
sections.text:
Preflight the merged configuration After merging the starter settings into your test checkout’s smu.toml, run the blueprint doctor and adapter preflight. Review the generated artifacts, required commands, unsupported modules, and fallback decisions. Run with SMU_HOME_DIR pointing at your test blueprint if your usual checkout is elsewhere. If a module falls back to rcm, decide whether that is acceptable for the current migration phase. If it is blocked, check whether the required tooling is installed and whether module.toml publishes an implementation for the target adapter and platform. SMU_HOME_DIR="$PWD" smu blueprint doctor --strict --json
SMU_HOME_DIR="$PWD" smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter hybrid --profile default --json

sections.title: Test one host before removing fallback
sections.text: Test one host before removing fallback On your test host, apply the adapter and profile that passed preflight. The apply step prepares generated artifacts and runs the adapter operations. Check that the expected configuration appears and that a fresh shell, editor, or other affected application starts correctly. Keep the previous blueprint commit available and review rollback coverage before changing a primary machine. Repeat the comparison as you port modules. Once each required module has an appropriate Nix implementation, test without rcm fallback and preflight again before switching additional machines. Author or adapt a module Updates and rollback SMU_HOME_DIR="$PWD" smu provisioning-adapter apply --adapter hybrid --profile default

title: Review a setup plan
description: Read a plan as a review of sources, module selection, conflicts, and expected writes before applying a setup.

sections.title: What a plan is for
sections.text: What a plan is for A plan gives you a concrete object to review before changing a machine. It connects the active blueprint, host, adapter, and module selection to the checks that smu can perform. Use it to catch a wrong checkout or unintended selection early. A plan does not execute every shell script to predict its effects. A module may invoke a package manager, contact a service, or inspect the host when it runs. Read its implementation and trust metadata alongside the report. smu plan --json

sections.title: Start with sources and identity
sections.text: Start with sources and identity Confirm that the blueprint checkout is the one you intended to use. Check its remote, branch or revision, and destination before interpreting later findings. Configuration from a different fork can be valid and still describe the wrong setup. Distinguish the downloaded bootstrap installer from the CLI bundled in your blueprint. The bootstrap obtains the checkout; the pinned installer supplies the smu behavior you will use afterwards. Consult smu --help from that installed copy when a command differs from an example. Verify the first installation

sections.title: Check the selected modules and adapter
sections.text: Check the selected modules and adapter Compare the proposed modules with the role of the target machine. A workstation collection can be inappropriate for a server even if it is available in the checkout. When using a built-in machine preset, inspect that preset and its platform requirements first. If you use a named blueprint profile, preflight that exact profile and adapter. A valid profile name does not guarantee that every selected module publishes the required adapter implementation. smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter rcm --profile default --json Review intent before execution Blueprint Plan You   Resolve host, profile, and adapter   Show selection and findings   Correct configuration if needed   Review the revised plan Change the configuration when the intent is wrong, then generate the plan again.

sections.title: Interpret conflicts and unknown state
sections.text: Interpret conflicts and unknown state A conflict is a reason to inspect the source and destination, not to overwrite the destination immediately. Compare the content and decide which copy should be authoritative. Keep a backup before replacing a file you currently depend on. Unknown installation state means detection is incomplete. It is not equivalent to missing, and it is not proof of failure. Check the module implementation and inspect the actual package, link, or application before deciding to run it again. Review destination files and ownership. Read warnings about trust, secrets, and privilege use. Check what rollback coverage actually includes. Keep unresolved findings visible until you understand their consequence.

sections.title: Apply only the selection you reviewed
sections.text: Apply only the selection you reviewed Keep the same checkout, host, and selection between review and execution. If you edit a profile, change a submodule revision, or switch machines, generate a fresh report. The previous report describes the previous inputs. Begin with a small reviewed module or a test host. Read the command summary, inspect the changed path or installed tool, and then run the relevant doctor or status check. Record what you tested before expanding the setup. Discover and apply modules Build a setup routine

title: Build a repeatable setup routine
description: Turn a successful first installation into a small review, apply, and verify workflow you can run again with confidence.

sections.title: Establish a known working baseline
sections.text: Establish a known working baseline A baseline is a blueprint revision plus evidence that the setup works on a particular host. It is more useful than a list of installed packages because it records the intent, implementation sources, and verification you relied on. After a successful first run, save your configuration changes in Git and note the tests you performed. Keep machine-specific values separate from shared preferences, and keep sensitive files outside the repository. You should be able to explain which parts of the machine the blueprint owns. Understand the blueprint

sections.title: Before each change
sections.text:
Before each change Inspect checkout state and decide what you want to change. Avoid combining a module update, a large dotfile rewrite, and an adapter migration in the same first test. Smaller changes give you a clearer recovery boundary. Preview the affected selection and read the relevant scripts. If you are updating sources, use the update doctor and dry run before applying. Preserve local work before attempting an update. smu update doctor --json
smu update --all --dry-run --json

sections.title: Use a short review cycle
sections.text: Use a short review cycle Treat the plan as the start of a conversation with the machine: does it identify the expected sources and intended writes? Apply the smallest useful change, then inspect the specific result. Only expand the change when that first result is understood. A green status is useful evidence, but the consuming application is the final check. Configuration syntax, runtime plugins, and authentication can still require attention after provisioning completes. The repeatable setup loop Review Apply Verify   Approve a small selection   Check actual tools and files   Save evidence and plan the next change Keep each loop small enough that a failure has an identifiable cause and recovery path.

sections.title: Choose practical verification checks
sections.text: Choose practical verification checks Write down checks that relate to your goal. For a shell module, open a new shell and run a familiar command. For editor configuration, open a project and confirm the expected integration. For dotfiles, check the link destination and the application that reads it. Record incomplete checks instead of treating a successful command as complete acceptance. If a module has unknown state, explain the direct observation you used to decide whether it worked. Change Useful verification Package installation Start the executable and inspect its version. Dotfile link Inspect the destination, then launch the consuming application. Profile edit Confirm module selection and adapter coverage on the target host. Source update Run doctors and repeat the important application checks.

sections.title: Keep a recovery boundary
sections.text: Keep a recovery boundary Before a change, know which files or applications you would need to restore. Preview ledger rollback coverage when it applies, and keep separate backups where arbitrary script or package operations are outside that coverage. When something fails, preserve output and identify the first failing layer. Avoid using destructive reset or force options as routine cleanup. A partial run deserves inspection before a retry. Review update recovery Diagnose an unexpected result

title: Customize themes and prompts
description: Choose a color theme and shell prompt, see what controls the effective profile, and apply the choice to supported tools.

sections.title: Choose the right setting
sections.text:
Choose the right setting A theme provides colors for supported tools. A prompt profile chooses the shell prompt, such as the full Starship configuration or the native classic prompt. A preset saves a theme and prompt pair together. Use list before setting an ID. Available themes come from the installed colorscheme module, and available prompts and presets come from their manifests. The current selection is marked in the list. smu theme list
smu prompt list
smu preset list
smu profile

sections.title: Save your choices
sections.text:
Save your choices This example saves Nord and the classic shell prompt. Run the corresponding list commands first to confirm both IDs are present on your machine. The choices are saved in ~/.config/set-me-up/profile.env. Open a new terminal to check shell startup behavior. If an existing terminal still uses an old prompt, check the effective choice there and again in a new shell. smu theme set nord
smu prompt set classic
smu profile

sections.title: Apply the theme to supported tools
sections.text: Apply the theme to supported tools If you also want to update the tool adapters provided by the colorschemes module, apply the current theme. Review the active theme before running this command because it updates files for supported tools. You can also apply a theme as part of saving it with smu theme set <theme> --apply. Use a preset when you want a known theme and prompt combination. Setting a preset saves both choices. Add --apply when you also intend to provision the colorschemes module. smu theme apply

sections.title: Find which value wins
sections.text: Find which value wins For each choice, the environment variable takes precedence, followed by its machine-local TOML file, the saved profile, and the default. If smu says it saved a new value but the old value still appears, start by checking the environment in that terminal. Priority Theme example 1. Shell environment SMU_THEME 2. Machine-local file ~/.config/set-me-up/theme.toml 3. Saved profile ~/.config/set-me-up/profile.env 4. Default The installer’s default theme theme = "nord"

sections.title: Check the profile after changing it
sections.text:
Check the profile after changing it The theme doctor checks the selected theme’s support files. The prompt doctor checks whether the selected prompt has what it needs. Use the profile doctor to check resolved configuration and identify stale or missing generated state. When a generated target contains a different local configuration, preserve your file and review the conflict before asking the adapter to rewrite it. smu theme doctor nord
smu prompt doctor classic
smu profile doctor Troubleshoot configuration changes Trust and safety

title: Troubleshoot an installed setup
description: Find the failing layer, collect a useful health snapshot, and choose a recovery step based on what the installer actually reports.

sections.title: Confirm the shell and blueprint
sections.text:
Confirm the shell and blueprint Start in the terminal where the problem appears. Use command -v to see which smu the shell runs. An empty result means the command is unavailable on that shell’s PATH. Check that bootstrap completed and restart the shell before changing machine settings. Check SMU_HOME_DIR next. With no override, smu uses the set-me-up directory under your home directory. In a multi-checkout workflow, identify the active blueprint before you inspect files or retry a change. command -v smu
blueprint_dir="${SMU_HOME_DIR:-$HOME/set-me-up}"
printf "%s\n" "$blueprint_dir"
git -C "$blueprint_dir" status --short

sections.title: Collect read-only diagnostics
sections.text:
Collect read-only diagnostics The general doctor reports installer health, profile and adapter checks, conflicts, and update readiness. Use status to see module detection and update doctor for a problem specific to Git or submodule updates. Read the first failed check and its path before fixing anything. Status can infer whether a declarative package or an entry is present, but a shell module’s effects may require checking the resulting application or configuration directly. smu doctor --json
smu status --json
smu update doctor --json

sections.title: Match the symptom to the next check
sections.text: Match the symptom to the next check Use these checks to narrow the issue. Fix one cause at a time, then run the same check again so you can tell whether the repair worked. Symptom Next step Module is missing from the list Check the module name and host bucket. Use smu --list-modules --all to see whether it exists for a different platform. Dotfile points at an unexpected source Run smu --lsrc and inspect the tag order and active blueprint. Preflight reports an unavailable adapter Check supported hosts, required tools, and module adapter coverage. Update reports a dirty checkout Use Git status to find the local change. Commit or stash work you want to keep before retrying. Theme appears unchanged in a new terminal Run smu profile and inspect environment and machine-local overrides. Inspect rcm tags and links Resolve theme and prompt choices Review adapter support

sections.title: Preview the recovery
sections.text:
Preview the recovery If the original operation recorded a state event, the rollback doctor explains whether the event has automatic, partial, or manual recovery coverage. The dry run lets you see the proposed inverse steps before changing the host. Keep a copy of the current file or checkout before applying recovery. Use the run’s status and the affected application as your final checks. For script modules with manual recovery, inspect the module’s writes and restore only the paths it owns. smu rollback doctor --json
smu rollback --dry-run Review update and rollback steps

sections.title: Collect a report you can share
sections.text: Collect a report you can share A support bundle records versions, health checks, module status, and plan details. The redaction step masks recognized secret patterns. Read the resulting file before attaching it to an issue, and remove remaining private hostnames, repository names, paths, or any sensitive values. Include what you expected to happen, the exact command you ran, the first failed check, and what changed since the last successful run. A short reproducible sequence helps someone identify the failing layer. smu support bundle --redact --output support.json Handle diagnostics and secrets

sections.title: Find the failing layer before retrying
sections.text: Find the failing layer before retrying Start with the earliest relevant error, rather than the last line printed by a wrapper. Separate source retrieval, blueprint validation, module discovery, adapter coverage, execution, and application behavior. Each layer has different evidence and a different repair. A missing module can mean the checkout scope excluded its source. An unsupported adapter can mean the module exists but has no implementation for that adapter. A successful module can still need application-specific verification. These are different failures and should not all be handled by reinstalling the blueprint. Trace an unexpected result Checkout Plan / preflight Application   Confirm sources and configuration   Check selection, conflicts, and coverage   Inspect execution and resulting files   Recheck assumptions only if sources differ Preserve diagnostic output and narrow the failing layer before making another change.

sections.title: Write a useful reproduction
sections.text: Write a useful reproduction Describe the host platform, blueprint revision, selected profile or module, exact command, and first error. Explain what you expected and how you verified the actual result. Include whether this was a new machine, an update, or a retry after a partial run. Use a minimal module selection when reproducing the failure. Remove credentials from reports and check command output for private repository URLs or hostnames. A small reproducible case is easier to test than a complete dump of a personal setup. Understand trust and diagnostics

title: Updates and rollback
description: Preview updates to an installed setup, check readiness, and use the state ledger to inspect rollback coverage.

sections.title: Check update readiness
sections.text:
Check update readiness Use the update doctor to check the blueprint and installer checkouts. The full dry run previews the steps before changing files. In the doctor output, check the checkout paths and branches, sync status, and dirty state. A diverged branch needs review and reconciliation before a fast-forward can work. The dry run lists the actions it would attempt and does not promise those actions will succeed. A Git submodule normally sits at the commit pinned in the blueprint. If an installer update is blocked because its checkout is detached, review and update the installer pin in the blueprint repository before applying that blueprint revision. smu update doctor --json
smu update --all --dry-run --json Commit or stash local changes before updating. Keep force-reset out of the routine path because it discards local changes.

sections.title: Apply an update
sections.text: Apply an update Run the full pipeline to refresh the blueprint, installer, modules, and generated configuration. To update only one part, choose the blueprint, installer, or modules subcommand instead. The full pipeline updates the blueprint and bundled installer before refreshing modules and generated files. A failure can leave the earlier steps applied, so inspect the output and both checkouts before retrying. smu update --all

sections.title: Verify the update
sections.text:
Verify the update Run the repository doctor again to check checkout state. Use the general doctor to inspect the active configuration, including conflicts in generated adapter targets. If an update changed shell or terminal configuration, open a new session and check the tools that use those files before considering the update done. smu update doctor --json
smu doctor --json

sections.title: Inspect rollback coverage
sections.text:
Inspect rollback coverage The state ledger records module provision batches, uninstall batches, and adapter materialization. A rollback can restore captured adapter files or symlinks, or run the existing uninstall flow for the last module provision batch. Uninstall events are recorded for audit. Reinstalling removed package state can be lossy, so the ledger does not automatically roll those events back. The rollback doctor reports recent events and coverage. The JSON preview shows the selected event and the paths or actions it can restore. Check those details before rolling back an event, particularly on a host with locally edited configuration. smu rollback doctor --json
smu rollback --json

sections.title: Understand client update recovery
sections.text: Understand client update recovery The client update command uses a lock that records repository revisions, generated file fingerprints, and validation results. The client update rollback path uses that record. The general smu rollback command instead works from state ledger events such as provisioning and adapter writes. When a client update report shows config drift, compare the generated files with the intended profile before overwriting changes. If using a report destination, check the policy first because report mode can send its payload to a configured endpoint. Troubleshoot a failed update

sections.title: Treat an update as several checkpoints
sections.text: Treat an update as several checkpoints An update spans more than a Git pull. It can change the blueprint, installer, module sources, and generated configuration. Capture the working revisions and review dirty state first. After updating, inspect the output and run the relevant health checks before using the setup as the new baseline. When the pipeline stops, read the first failure and determine which earlier steps completed. Re-running a command without understanding that boundary can mix old assumptions with new sources. Preserve the output and checkout state while you diagnose it. Review, update, and verify You Checkouts Machine   Inspect readiness and revisions   Review the dry-run actions   Apply the selected update   Refresh supported configuration   Verify tools and generated files Updates are not a transaction across every package and repository; earlier completed steps may remain after a failure.

sections.title: Know what a rollback cannot restore
sections.text: Know what a rollback cannot restore Returning a repository to an earlier revision does not automatically uninstall packages or undo arbitrary commands that have already run. Likewise, a ledger rollback only covers the event and paths it reports. Compare the planned recovery with the actual effect you need to reverse. Keep independent backups for important configuration and user data. Before recovery, preserve new local changes and confirm which paths the operation owns. Check the application again afterwards; a successful rollback command is not proof that every external dependency was restored. Troubleshoot a partial setup

title: Headless VPS
description: Use the VPS setup profile on a headless Debian or Ubuntu machine, including a DigitalOcean Droplet.

sections.title: Prepare the host
sections.text:
Prepare the host Start on a headless Debian or Ubuntu host that you can reach over SSH. Use an account with sudo for installing system packages, and run the bootstrap as the user whose home directory will hold the blueprint. Install the tools below, then follow Quick start to configure your fork and download and inspect smu-bootstrap.sh. Keep SSH credentials and host-specific secrets outside the blueprint. sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y bash curl git ca-certificates python3 Download the bootstrap

sections.title: Preview the platform bootstrap
sections.text: Preview the platform bootstrap Select platform submodules to limit what the bootstrap checks out. Review the repository, branch, destination, and submodule scope. Platform scope keeps shared repositories and the Debian module checkout where your blueprint declares them. It skips the Mac-specific module checkouts. The plan’s submodule_scope value should be platform. SMU_SUBMODULE_SCOPE=platform bash smu-bootstrap.sh --no-header --plan --json

sections.title: Install the blueprint
sections.text: Install the blueprint Use the same platform scope when you run the reviewed bootstrap. Open the checkout in the current SSH session and verify the bundled CLI as shown in Quick start. If the smu command is unavailable, use the temporary Bash function from that guide. SMU_SUBMODULE_SCOPE=platform bash smu-bootstrap.sh --no-header

sections.title: Plan server provisioning
sections.text: Plan server provisioning Inspect the VPS profile, modules, and expected changes before provisioning. Look for the server/headless module, then review its package list and any conflict, secret, or trust findings. If that module cannot be resolved, check whether dotfiles/modules/debian is initialized before retrying. smu plan --machine vps --json

sections.title: Apply the server profile
sections.text: Apply the server profile Use the vps profile for the targeted server setup. It provisions the Debian server/headless module instead of the workstation package set. This command can install Debian packages and prompt for sudo. Run it after checking the plan and reviewing the server/headless package list. smu --setup-profile vps

sections.title: Verify the server setup
sections.text: Verify the server setup Check the Debian module in the status output and review any partial or missing package entries. If the setup profile rejects the host, check that the machine is a Debian or Ubuntu system rather than retrying with a workstation profile. smu status --search server/headless --json Machine profiles Troubleshoot a setup

sections.title: Choose a Nix path if needed
sections.text: Choose a Nix path if needed Use Home Manager for user-level provisioning when Nix and Home Manager are installed on the host. Use the NixOS adapter only on a NixOS host. The server setup command above follows the rcm provisioning path for the Debian baseline module. For a Nix-managed setup, select the Nix adapter in smu.toml and use its separate preflight and apply workflow. Provisioning adapters Trust and safety

title: Guides
description: Learn how to build, review, and adapt a repeatable setup from the files and modules in your blueprint.

sections.title: Build your setup
sections.text: Build your setup Start by understanding where configuration lives and how the installer resolves module implementations. These guides take you from a blueprint fork to a small, reviewed setup you can verify on one machine. Blueprints Modules Review a setup plan

sections.title: Customize the pieces
sections.text: Customize the pieces Bring your own dotfiles, add a focused module, and separate the responsibilities of your machines. Keep preferences and platform differences explicit so you can review them before the next installation. Organize and link dotfiles Author a module Choose machine profiles Customize themes and prompts

sections.title: Adapt an existing setup
sections.text: Adapt an existing setup Recheck coverage when changing adapters or moving to a new host. A versioned blueprint makes your intent portable; the new environment still needs its own compatibility and acceptance checks. Migrate toward Nix Move to a new machine

title: Operations
description: Keep an installed setup healthy: update it, verify changes, diagnose failures, and plan for additional hosts.

sections.title: Maintain a working setup
sections.text: Maintain a working setup Use a short review, apply, and verify cycle. Understand the update boundary and rollback coverage before changing a machine that already works. Build a repeatable setup routine Updates and rollback Troubleshoot an installed setup

sections.title: Operate servers and multiple hosts
sections.text: Operate servers and multiple hosts Use the headless path for Debian or Ubuntu servers and validate each host rather than assuming that a shared blueprint makes every environment identical. Headless VPS Plan a fleet of hosts

title: Overview
description: Define your setup in a version-controlled blueprint, then use smu to apply the modules each machine needs.

sections.title: Choose a setup path
sections.text: Choose a setup path Choose Quick start when you want to bring your personal tools and dotfiles to a workstation. For a fresh Debian or Ubuntu server over SSH, use the Headless VPS guide for a smaller package baseline. Start with the rcm path when your blueprint uses shell modules, package lists, and dotfile symlinks. Check Provisioning adapters if you already manage your user environment or operating system with Nix. Quick start Headless VPS Provisioning adapters

sections.title: How it fits together
sections.text: How it fits together The blueprint is your Git repository. It contains dotfiles, module selections, and the settings that tell smu how to provision them. The bootstrap downloads that repository and its selected submodules, including a bundled copy of the installer. A module is a unit of work, such as a package list or a setup script. A profile selects a group of modules, while an adapter determines how to apply them. For example, a desktop profile can use Home Manager for modules that publish Nix definitions and rcm for a shell module during a hybrid migration. From blueprint to provisioned machine You Blueprint bootstrap smu   Review and preview   Install the chosen blueprint   Set up the CLI   Plan and apply selected modules Keep your blueprint under version control and review changes before applying them.

sections.title: A typical setup session
sections.text: A typical setup session Review the target repository and the scripts it runs. Install the blueprint into the directory you intend to keep, then use the bundled CLI to inspect the profile and module state. Apply one reviewed module first. Check that it did what you expected before adding the rest. When you move to another machine, start with the same blueprint and choose the profile that fits that host. Customize dotfiles Choose a machine profile

sections.title: Maintain a setup
sections.text: Maintain a setup Check what a module changes before applying it. Preview updates to an installed checkout before switching to new configuration. Use the status report to distinguish missing packages from script modules that have no detection marker. If an update is blocked by local work or a provisioning step fails, review the relevant diagnostic before retrying. Choose modules Update a setup Trust and safety Troubleshoot a setup

sections.title: Continue with a guided workflow
sections.text: Continue with a guided workflow Use the guides below once you understand the basic blueprint and module flow. They cover the review decisions around a setup, the differences to recheck on another host, and the verification routine that makes future changes predictable. Review a setup plan Move to a new machine Build a repeatable setup routine

title: Quick start
description: Set up your first machine. Choose a blueprint, review the bootstrap, verify the installed CLI, and try one module.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.text: Before you start Use a macOS, Debian or Ubuntu, or Arch machine with Bash, curl, Git, and Python 3 available. The examples use Bash syntax. Run them in the same Bash session so the blueprint settings and the temporary smu function stay available. Choose a destination before running the bootstrap. It defaults to $HOME/set-me-up. For a custom destination, choose a path whose parent directory exists, export SMU_HOME_DIR, and keep using it in later sessions. Some module scripts use the default path directly, so review them before choosing a custom one. On macOS, complete any required Xcode Command Line Tools and Rosetta setup first. The bootstrap can attempt those prerequisite installations before it reaches --plan or --doctor. command -v bash curl git python3

sections.title: Fork and configure a blueprint
sections.text: Fork and configure a blueprint Fork smeltery/set-me-up-blueprint on GitHub and note the owner, repository, and branch of the fork. Choose the branch that contains the files you want on this machine. The stock blueprint includes an rcm profile and a minimal example module. Inspect smu.toml, .gitmodules, and dotfiles/modules/install.sh in the fork. Review any module or dotfile changes before you install them. Keep credentials and host secrets outside the repository. Blueprint layout

sections.title: Download and inspect the bootstrap
sections.text:
Download and inspect the bootstrap Replace the example owner, repository, and branch with your actual fork. Use the branch name as shown on GitHub. If curl returns 404, verify the branch, path, and repository access before proceeding. Read the downloaded bootstrap and check the installer source referenced by SMU_INSTALLER_URL or SMU_INSTALLER_REF. Review the code it delegates to as well. Downloading from a branch follows the version currently at that branch, so check again if the source changes. export SMU_BLUEPRINT="your-account/your-blueprint"
export SMU_BLUEPRINT_BRANCH="main"
BOOTSTRAP_URL="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${SMU_BLUEPRINT}/${SMU_BLUEPRINT_BRANCH}/dotfiles/modules/install.sh"
curl -fL "$BOOTSTRAP_URL" -o smu-bootstrap.sh
less smu-bootstrap.sh

sections.title: Preview the installation
sections.text:
Preview the installation The plan reports the target repository, branch, destination, installer reference, and submodule scope. The doctor also reports the state and readiness of an existing destination. Check blueprint.repo, blueprint.branch, and blueprint.path against your intended checkout. Look at installer.ref and submodule_scope to see which bootstrap source and checkout scope you selected. A new destination normally reports missing and ready. If the existing path reports blocked-dirty, preserve your local work before retrying. For blocked-not-git, pick another directory or inspect the existing contents before proceeding. bash smu-bootstrap.sh --no-header --plan --json
bash smu-bootstrap.sh --no-header --doctor --json The preview reports the target without cloning or updating the blueprint. It still runs the reviewed bootstrap and its prerequisite checks.

sections.title: Install the blueprint
sections.text: Install the blueprint Run the installer once the destination and source match your plan. It prompts before obtaining the blueprint. A new setup clones the requested branch and initializes its selected submodules. An existing clean checkout is updated with a fast-forward. The bootstrap writes a local set-me-up profile. Provision the modules you want as a separate step. bash smu-bootstrap.sh --no-header

sections.title: Verify the checkout and CLI
sections.text:
Verify the checkout and CLI Confirm the remote and branch in the checkout. If smu is not on PATH, the function below runs the Python CLI from the bundled installer. It applies only to this Bash session and also works with a custom SMU_HOME_DIR. The installer shown in the bootstrap plan is the script that obtains your blueprint. The CLI comes from the set-me-up-installer submodule pinned by that blueprint. Check smu --help to see what the installed version supports. export SMU_HOME_DIR="${SMU_HOME_DIR:-$HOME/set-me-up}"
git -C "$SMU_HOME_DIR" remote get-url origin
git -C "$SMU_HOME_DIR" branch --show-current
smu() {
  python3 "$SMU_HOME_DIR/set-me-up-installer/smu.py" "$@"
}
smu --help

sections.title: Find modules for this machine
sections.text:
Find modules for this machine List the modules in your checkout and check their state. The normal list includes the current operating system bucket and universal modules. Use a name from the list when selecting a platform module. For a small first run on the stock blueprint, try the example module in the Modules guide. It is a script skeleton, so you can check the provisioning workflow without selecting a package collection. On a headless Debian or Ubuntu machine, use the VPS guide instead. smu --list-modules
smu status --json Choose and apply modules Set up a headless VPS Troubleshoot an install

sections.title: Finish with an acceptance check
sections.text: Finish with an acceptance check An installed checkout is not the same as a fully configured workstation. Confirm that smu resolves to the intended bundled installer, that the selected module completed, and that the tool or file it manages behaves as expected. Keep the scope of the first run deliberately small. Write down what you verified and what remains manual, such as credentials or an application sign-in. This gives you a concrete next step rather than an ambiguous claim that the machine is done. A successful first setup Review sources Install blueprint Verify one module   Confirm destination and source   Use the bundled CLI   Inspect the actual result Only expand the setup after the initial checkout and a small module run are understood. Review plans in detail Keep a repeatable routine

title: Provisioning adapters
description: Provisioning adapters determine how smu applies a blueprint. Choose one for the host and the capabilities published by its modules.

sections.title: Available adapters
sections.text: Available adapters Choose an adapter based on the host and the module implementations available in the blueprint. rcm is the traditional path for shell scripts, Brewfiles, package lists, and symlinks. A Nix adapter requires its corresponding tools and modules that declare the adapter. The global adapter in smu.toml is a default. A named profile can override it. The profile also selects the modules, so checking an adapter by itself does not confirm that every module in the profile is supported. Adapter Use it for rcm Shell modules, package lists, Brewfiles, and rcm symlinks. home-manager Nix user environments on supported Linux and macOS hosts. nix-darwin Nix-managed macOS system configuration. nixos System configuration on a NixOS host. hybrid A Nix adapter with rcm fallback for legacy modules.

sections.title: Check adapter support
sections.text:
Check adapter support Capabilities describe the supported host families and requirements. Preflight checks the chosen profile and its modules before apply. Review host_supported, can_apply, and errors first. Read plan for the proposed commands and generated paths. A missing-module error points to the checkout or module name. A missing-adapter error points to a module that cannot supply the selected implementation. The Home Manager example assumes it is installed and the default profile includes modules that publish Home Manager definitions. For an rcm profile, substitute rcm. For NixOS, run checks on an actual NixOS host. smu provisioning-adapter capabilities --json
smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter home-manager --profile default --json

sections.title: Configure a hybrid migration
sections.text:
Configure a hybrid migration Pick the Nix implementation and decide whether legacy rcm modules may fall back. Set allow_rcm_fallback to false for a profile that must be fully backed by the Nix adapter. A hybrid plan shows which modules use the Nix adapter and which fall back to rcm. Review the fallback group so you know which module scripts or package lists can still run. [provisioning]
adapter = "hybrid"
nix_adapter = "home-manager"
allow_rcm_fallback = true Blueprint layout Headless VPS Plan a Nix migration

sections.title: Diagnose a failed preflight
sections.text: Diagnose a failed preflight  Finding What to check Host unsupported Choose an adapter that supports this operating system. NixOS is for a NixOS host. No modules selected Check the named profile and its modules in smu.toml. Module missing Confirm the module name and checkout before changing adapters. Adapter missing Use a compatible module, add the adapter implementation, or deliberately allow rcm fallback in a hybrid profile.

title: CLI reference
description: Use smu to discover modules, inspect a blueprint, apply changes, and maintain an installed setup.

sections.title: Common commands
sections.text: Common commands Run smu --help on the installed machine for the available flags. The table groups frequently used commands by task. Commands with output such as status, plan, or diff are useful before applying a change. Use the bundled Python CLI from Quick start when you need to target a specific checkout or want to avoid setup work performed by the legacy shell wrapper. Command What it does Effect smu --list-modules List available modules for the host. Inspect smu status --json Report installed and missing modules. Inspect smu plan --machine vps --json Preview the server setup. Preview smu diff example Preview module changes for the named module. Preview smu --provision --no-base --modules example Apply only the named module. Apply smu update --all --dry-run Preview the update pipeline. Preview smu --setup-profile vps Apply the headless server setup. Apply

sections.title: Target the intended checkout
sections.text:
Target the intended checkout The Python CLI uses SMU_HOME_DIR, or $HOME/set-me-up if it is unset, to find the blueprint. Keep the variable set when running from a non-default directory. Check which smu your shell resolves if the command appears to read a different setup. type smu
printf "%s\n" "${SMU_HOME_DIR:-$HOME/set-me-up}" Run the bundled CLI

sections.title: Inspect or manage rcm symlinks
sections.text: Inspect or manage rcm symlinks With rcm installed, use --lsrc to list files that would be symlinked, --rcup to link them, or --rcdn to remove links. Review the source and destination paths from --lsrc. The apply and removal flags change symlinks, so use them after checking that the dotfiles directory points at the intended checkout. smu --lsrc

sections.title: Use structured output
sections.text:
Use structured output Use --json on commands that support it to collect structured status and preflight data. Check the installed version’s help before depending on a flag in automation. A JSON report can describe a failure even when it is valid JSON. Check the exit status and report-specific fields before running dependent commands. In adapter preflight, inspect can_apply and errors. For status, read the modules list and retain unknown as a separate state. Trust and safety Updates and rollback smu status --json
smu provisioning-adapter preflight --adapter rcm --profile default --json

title: Trust and safety
description: Review the sources and proposed system changes before installing a blueprint or applying a module.

sections.title: Review the sources you run
sections.text: Review the sources you run Read your bootstrap, its delegated installer, and any selected module script before running them. Review packages and write targets, and keep host secrets outside the blueprint. Start with the exact fork and branch you plan to run. Read its .gitmodules entries, then review the scripts and package definitions for the selected modules. Check whether a package manager command, network request, sudo prompt, or write outside your home directory is expected. Keep SSH keys, tokens, and machine-specific credentials outside tracked dotfiles. Use a secure source appropriate to the host, such as the VPS provider’s secret mechanism or your normal secrets manager.

sections.title: Inspect module trust metadata
sections.text:
Inspect module trust metadata A module can publish trust details in module.toml, such as its trust classification, network and sudo requirements, expected writes, and rollback coverage. Treat this information as a description supplied by the module author. Read the implementation to confirm the declared network, write, and privilege requirements. Missing trust metadata is reported as unspecified. trust = "first-party"
network = true
requires_sudo = false
writes = ["~/.config/git"]
rollback = "partial"

sections.title: Run read-only checks
sections.text:
Run read-only checks A plan summarizes the intended blueprint, adapter, modules, and changes. Run the doctor commands to surface trust and secret findings before applying. Read the plan’s module and package operations, adapter conflicts, secret findings, trust warnings, and rollback coverage. For a machine other than the VPS example, choose its profile or omit --machine to plan from the configured blueprint. The secret check looks for common names and value patterns. Review the reported paths directly and investigate warnings before applying changes. smu plan --machine vps --json
smu trust doctor --json
smu secrets doctor --json
smu doctor --strict --json

sections.title: Redact diagnostic reports
sections.text: Redact diagnostic reports Use the redacted support bundle option and review its contents before sharing it. The bundle writes a local file containing health, version, and setup details. Redaction covers known credential patterns. Review the entire file before sharing, including repository paths, host details, and module names. smu support bundle --redact --output support.json Updates and rollback
